answers.answer: He arrived late on the night of 4 May, just after midnight, so the arrival falls on 5 May 1893. He left Bistritz on 4 May, St George's Eve; on the coach he checked his watch 'within a few minutes of midnight'; and his journal entry describing the castle courtyard and the Count's welcome is dated 5 May.

Dr John Seward. Lucy knew him before the story: he proposed to her on 24 May. He had also known Van Helsing for years. In his letter of 2 September Seward calls Van Helsing 'my old friend and master', and Van Helsing's reply recalls Seward sucking the gangrene poison from his wound. No other character is shown knowing both beforehand.

The question's premise is wrong. By 30 September nothing was attacking Lucy. She had died around 20 September, and the group destroyed her as Un-Dead on the night of 29 September. On 30 September they understood that a vampire, the Count, had preyed on her. At that evening's council Van Helsing says 'There are such beings as vampires' and regrets that 'one so precious life' could have been spared. Seward wishes they had known about Carfax sooner: 'we might have saved poor Lucy!'

(1) That the small wounds on the Hampstead children came from whatever had wounded Lucy. On 26 Sept Van Helsing said 'They were made by Miss Lucy!' Seward called him mad and gave way only to evidence. (2) That Lucy's empty coffin meant a body-snatcher or undertaker's men had taken her (26 Sept). He dropped this after seeing a white figure with a child in the churchyard, then on 27 Sept finding her in the coffin rosy and undecayed after a week, with teeth 'sharper than before'. He accepted the idea ('Do not press me too hard... I am willing to accept'). (3) On 28 Sept he fell back again, calling Van Helsing's ideas 'outrages on common sense', wondering if the Professor was unhinged and had done it himself. He gave that up on 29 Sept when he saw Un-Dead Lucy with the child, eyes 'full of hell-fire'. (4) Smaller ones: on 30 Sept he regrets that it 'never struck me' Carfax next door was the Count's lair, though Renfield gave clues. On 1 Oct he had believed Renfield's 'reason had been restored', but held back when Renfield's frantic pleading began.

Fifty boxes ('Fifty cases of common earth') went from the castle to Whitby and were all delivered to the chapel at Carfax. In the end: 29 stayed at Carfax and were sterilised with the Host on 3 Oct. Six went to 197 Chicksand Street, Mile End New Town, and six to Jamaica Lane, Bermondsey; Godalming and Morris destroyed both lots. Nine went to the Piccadilly house, where the group found and destroyed only eight. The ninth was the Count's last earth-box. He shipped it out of London on the Czarina Catherine and went back to Transylvania in it, and the gypsies were carrying it toward the castle when he was killed in it on 6 Nov. (29+6+6+9 = 50.)

On 26 July 1893, in Mina Murray's journal: Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep.' Mrs Westenra had raised it with Mina, and they agreed Mina would lock their door each night. Mrs Westenra added that Lucy's father had the same habit. Exact searches for sleep-walking or 'in her sleep' found nothing earlier.

In the store, only Lucy's diary entry of 12 September (Hillingham, the night of the garlic flowers). Her other eight documents all name Arthur: the letters of 9 May (Wednesday) and 24 May, the Whitby letter of 30 Aug (filed under 19 Aug), the diary entries of 24 Aug, 25 Aug, 9 Sept and 17 Sept, and the memorandum of 17 Sept night ('Good-bye, dear Arthur').

In Jonathan Harker's journal, entry dated 5 May 1893: 'Listen to them--the children of the night. What music they make!' He says it on Harker's first night at the castle, in the late hours of 4-5 May.

experience: Three things helped most. `list` and `grep` give exact counts and dated one-line heads, and the date/narrator/document header on every hit let me plan the next step without reading whole passages. `list --after 1893-09-30 --before 1893-09-30` returned '27 passages match (9 entries)'. That showed me at a glance that Lucy was gone by then and the Q3 premise was false. For Q7, `list --source lucy` ('17 passages match (9 entries)') next to `grep "Arthur" --source lucy` ('9 passages match (8 entries)') made it a set difference, leaving e0106.1. For Q5, grep "earth-box" turned up 'There is but one more earth-box', which accounted for the ninth Piccadilly box. Things that got in the way: I never saw a semantic-exception message, despite the help text promising them. When `search` ranked badly (my Seward 'retraction' query returned four empty 'DR. SEWARD’S DIARY' header passages, each scoring 0.6741), nothing flagged them as content-free. Some metadata is wrong. e0081.1 is dated 1893-08-19 but the letter reads 'Whitby, 30 August'. e0085.1 is filed 08-23 but reads '24 August'. A 5 November passage in the voice of Van Helsing's memorandum is labelled 'Dr. Seward'. So the date filters cannot be fully trusted. I wished `grep` could OR terms (sleep-walk | sleepwalk | walking in her sleep), and that `list` could group by entry to show which entries lack a term. Then Q7 would be one command.
